title: About
text:
Every pitch a batter sees is compared with what an average batter would have produced against the same pitch type, in the same count and at the same location. The value is expressed in runs (change in the inning’s run expectancy) per 100 pitches.

Decision: the value of choosing to swing or take, compared with the league’s average choice on that pitch. A called strike or a ball does not change the credit: only the choice counts, not the umpire’s call.
Execution: what the batter gets out of his swings (whiff, foul or ball in play). A ball in play is valued by its exit velocity and launch angle (xwOBA), not by its actual outcome, which removes the effect of defense and luck.
PCV: the sum of the two.

Results are then split into 12 cells (4 pitch families × 3 count states) and shrunk toward the mean according to the number of pitches in each cell. A batter’s overall value averages the cells with the same weights for everyone, which corrects for some batters seeing many more two-strike pitches than others.
Families: fastballs (four-seam, sinker, cutter), sliders (including sweepers), curveballs, changeups (including splitters).

title: About
text:
Reliability
Over one season, PCV has a reliability of 0.69, decision 0.84 and execution 0.70 (correlation between even and odd games, stepped up to a full season). For comparison, the same statistic computed from actual rather than expected outcomes reaches only 0.35.

title: About
text:
Updates
The site is recomputed every week during the regular season. Data through September 27, 2026.

Data

title: Count sensitivity
text:
Count sensitivity compares a batter with two strikes and in hitter’s counts, against the same pitch type. It first removes what his overall level predicts: a whiff costs more with two strikes, so a weak hitter falls further behind there without it being specific to the count. A positive value means the batter holds up relatively better with two strikes than ahead in the count; a negative value, that he falls off more than expected.
These differences are small and noisy. Over one season, the most reliable sensitivity this year is decision against fastballs (reliability 0.50); it is the only one charted.

title: Count sensitivity
text:
Reliability
Correlation between even and odd games, stepped up to a full season (Spearman-Brown). Above about 0.5, a measure mostly separates talent; below 0.2, it mostly reflects chance.
